title: Wyatt's version of Pace non trovo
greek: Pace non trovo, et non ò da far guerra
short: Sir Thomas Wyatt's English version of Rvf 134, printed by Bohn from Harington's Nugae Antiquae rather than from Wyatt's own manuscript.
body: Petrarch's 'Pace non trovo, et non ò da far guerra' ('I find no peace, and have no means to make war') is the most famous catalogue of the lover's contradictions. Sir Thomas Wyatt (1503-1542), who with Surrey brought the sonnet into English, translated it in the 1520s or 1530s; it survives in the Egerton manuscript (BL Egerton MS 2711) and was printed in Tottel's Songes and Sonettes (1557). Bohn (1879) footnotes 'Harrington's Nugae Antiquae', the eighteenth-century printing of the Harington family papers, and its text differs from the Egerton text followed by modern editors in several readings (see the notes on 'lacketh', 'none occasion', 'pleaseth' and 'greif'). The archive keeps the old spelling of Bohn's source.

title: all my warre is done
short: Wyatt's 'all my war is done' differs from Petrarch's 'non ò da far guerra', 'I have nothing to make war with'.
body: Petrarch's speaker has no peace yet no means of fighting; Wyatt's has no peace although the war is over, or (on another reading of 'done') no peace and his whole life is war being waged. Editors note the ambiguity of 'done': 'finished', or 'being done, carried on'. Either way the line sets up the first of the poem's paradoxes, which are the sonnet's whole structure.

title: antithesis and paradox
short: The poem is built of antitheses, each line pairing contraries, the rhetorical signature of Petrarchan love poetry.
body: Petrarch's 'e temo, et spero; et ardo, et son un ghiaccio' piles up pairs joined by 'and'. The figure is antithesis, and its compressed form, oxymoron, gave English the 'icy fire' and 'freezing fire' of later Elizabethan sonneteers. Wyatt keeps the list form and the insistent conjunctions ('and... yet... nor'), but his lines are rougher than Petrarch's hendecasyllables, with variable stress and syllable count. Whether that roughness is deliberate or the result of an English metre not yet settled is an old debate in Wyatt criticism.

title: I bourne and freese lyke yse
short: Petrarch: 'et ardo, et son un ghiaccio', I burn and am a block of ice. The old spellings are 'burn', 'freeze', 'like', 'ice'.
body: Fire and ice are the most famous Petrarchan contraries: the lover burns with desire and freezes with fear or despair, often at once. Petrarch says he 'is' ice; Wyatt makes it a simile, 'freeze like ice'. The spellings here (bourne, freese, yse) are sixteenth-century forms and should be read as modern burn, freeze, ice. The paradox has classical roots: Sappho's fragment 31 already joins a thin fire under the skin with cold sweat and trembling.

anchor: I flye above the wynde, yet cannot ryse
title: above the wind
greek: volo sopra 'l cielo, et giaccio in terra
short: Petrarch has the lover fly above the heavens and lie on the earth; Wyatt brings the heights down to 'the wind'.
body: The Italian 'et volo sopra 'l cielo, et giaccio in terra' ('I fly above the sky, and lie upon the ground') sets heaven against earth. Wyatt's 'above the wind' is less cosmic, and he turns the second half from lying on the ground to the inability to rise. Muir and Thomson's text and Rebholz's read 'yet can I not arise'; Bohn's 'yet cannot ryse' is smoother.

title: season (seize on)
greek: et nulla stringo, et tutto 'l mondo abbraccio
short: 'Season' here is an old spelling of 'seize on', not the modern word: 'I have nothing, yet I seize the whole world.'
body: Petrarch writes 'et nulla stringo, et tutto 'l mondo abbraccio' ('I clasp nothing, and embrace the whole world'). In the Egerton manuscript Wyatt's word is spelt 'seson', which modern editors print as 'seize on' (Rebholz). The verb is related to the legal term seisin, possession of land; the spelling 'season' in Bohn's source looks like the modern word but is not. The rhyme with 'pryson' and 'occasion' depends on the older pronunciation.

title: looseth nor lacketh
short: Modern editions read 'locketh': the one who neither unlocks nor locks holds me in prison. Bohn's 'lacketh' is a corrupt reading.
body: Petrarch's line is 'Tal m'à in pregion, che non m'apre né serra', 'one holds me in prison who neither opens nor locks'. The Egerton text, followed by Rebholz and by Muir and Thomson, reads 'That loseth nor locketh', loosens nor locks, which exactly translates 'apre' and 'serra'. The reading 'lacketh' in Bohn's text (taken from Harington's Nugae Antiquae) makes poor sense and is best explained as a misreading of 'locketh'. The jailer is Love, or the lady.

title: the prison of love
short: Love as prison is a medieval commonplace; here the prisoner is neither kept nor released.
body: Petrarch's next line, 'né per suo mi riten né scioglie il laccio' ('neither keeps me as its own nor loosens the noose'), completes the paradox, which Wyatt renders 'And holdes me not, yet can I escape no wyse'. The image of love's prison goes back to the Roman de la Rose and beyond. Some readers connect Wyatt's version with his own imprisonments in the Tower of London (1536 and 1541), but the image is Petrarch's, and the dating of the translation is uncertain, so the biographical reading is at best an overtone.

title: no wyse
short: 'No wise' means 'in no way, by no means'; the noun wise (manner) survives in 'otherwise' and 'likewise'.
body: The phrase 'in no wise' was ordinary in Tudor English (the King James Bible uses it often, as in 'he shall in no wise lose his reward', Matthew 10:42). Wyatt's 'yet can I escape no wise' means 'yet I can in no way escape'. The same noun appears in 'Lykewyse' in line 13. The archive's spelling 'wyse' is a sixteenth-century form, like 'yse' and 'ryse' in the octave, and should be read as modern 'wise'.

title: at my device
short: 'Device' here means will or choice: Love neither lets me live nor die as I would wish.
body: In older English 'device' could mean 'will, desire, pleasure' (OED, device, n.), so 'at my device' means 'as I choose'. Petrarch's lines 7-8 read 'et non m'ancide Amore, et non mi sferra, / né mi vuol vivo, né mi trae d'impaccio' ('Love does not kill me, nor unshackle me; he does not want me alive, nor free me from my plight'). Wyatt compresses the two lines and moves 'Love' out of the sentence: the subject throughout is an unnamed 'that'.

title: of death it giveth none occasion
short: Bohn's text reads 'none occasion'; the Egerton text reads 'giveth me occasion'. The two readings say opposite things.
body: In Rebholz's Egerton-based text the line is 'And yet of death it giveth me occasion': love gives me cause to die, though it will not let me die. Bohn's reading, 'giveth none occasion', means love gives me no way out through death, which is closer to Petrarch's 'né mi trae d'impaccio' ('nor frees me from my plight'). The variant is a good instance of how much Wyatt's texts depend on which witness is followed. Students quoting the poem should name the edition.

title: playne (plain)
greek: Veggio senza occhi, et non ò lingua et grido; Lat. plangere
short: 'Plain' is the old verb 'to complain, lament'; Petrarch: 'Veggio senza occhi, et non ò lingua et grido'.
body: Petrarch: 'I see without eyes, and have no tongue, and cry out'. Wyatt's 'plain' (from Old French plaindre, Latin plangere) means to lament aloud, the root of 'complaint' and 'plaintive' (OED, plain, v.1). The paradox of seeing without eyes may mean seeing the beloved in imagination, and crying without a tongue the poet's written laments. Egerton reads 'Without eyen', with the old plural.

anchor: I love another, and yet I hate my self
title: love of another, hatred of self
greek: et ò in odio me stesso, et amo altrui
short: Petrarch: 'et ò in odio me stesso, et amo altrui'. Wyatt reverses the order and Egerton reads 'and thus I hate myself'.
body: Petrarch places self-hatred first. Wyatt puts love first, and in the Egerton text the conjunction 'thus' makes self-hatred the consequence of love; Bohn's 'and yet' keeps it as one more paradox. The theme, love of another as self-loss, is central to Petrarch's penitential frame (compare Rvf 1, where the lover blushes at himself). The figure recalls Catullus 85, 'odi et amo' ('I hate and I love'), the classical model for such self-division.

title: I feed in sorrow
short: Petrarch: 'Pascomi di dolor, piangendo rido', I feed myself on grief, laugh while weeping.
body: The lover nourished by pain recurs throughout the Canzoniere (compare the heart fed on sighs in Rvf 1). Wyatt's 'laugh in all my pain' loses Petrarch's tight oxymoron 'piangendo rido' (weeping I laugh), spreading it across a looser phrase. Egerton reads 'I feed me in sorrow', with the reflexive pronoun that matches 'Pascomi'. Wyatt's 'laugh' also loses the grammatical simultaneity of Petrarch's gerund, in which weeping and laughing happen at the same moment.

anchor: pleaseth me both death and lyf
title: pleaseth / displeaseth
greek: egualmente mi spiace morte et vita
short: Petrarch: 'egualmente mi spiace morte et vita', death and life displease me equally. Bohn's 'pleaseth' inverts this; Egerton reads 'displeaseth'.
body: The Egerton text (Rebholz) reads 'Likewise displeaseth me both life and death', which exactly translates 'spiace'. Bohn's version, from Harington, says that both please him, which still makes a paradox but reverses Petrarch's sense, and it puts death first, as Petrarch does. Whether the Harington reading is a scribal slip or a different stage of the poem cannot be settled from the printed sources; modern editors prefer Egerton.

title: the closing couplet
greek: in questo stato son, donna, per voi
short: Wyatt ends with a rhymed couplet and drops Petrarch's last words, 'donna, per voi' ('lady, because of you').
body: Petrarch's sonnet closes 'in questo stato son, donna, per voi' ('in this state I am, lady, because of you'), turning at last to the woman. Wyatt replaces the address with an inward conclusion, 'my delight is causer of my grief' (Egerton: 'of this strife'), so that the cause lies in the lover's own pleasure. Formally, his sestet rhymes CDDC EE, ending in the couplet that became the mark of the English sonnet. The octave keeps Petrarch's ABBA ABBA, though with half-rhymes (done, season, pryson, occasion) that may reflect older pronunciation.
